spots.name: Belém Tower
spots.label: Belém Tower

text.access_note: The promenade and gardens are open public space, but going inside the tower may be ticketed or restricted, and the interior was reported closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Belém Tower stands on the north bank of the Tagus in Belém, in the west of Lisbon, close to the Jerónimos Monastery. It sits at the water's edge, with a riverside promenade and gardens beside it.
text.description: Belém Tower is a small, ornate fortress standing at the edge of the Tagus, and it is one of the easiest buildings in Lisbon to photograph. It was finished in 1519 and built from local lioz limestone. It is made up of a low bastion and a four-storey tower about 30 metres high. The carved stonework, domed turrets and sculpted crosses give it plenty of detail, and the river behind it gives a clean, open background. It was built to guard the mouth of the river and to greet the ships of Portuguese explorers returning home, and today it is listed by UNESCO together with the nearby Jerónimos Monastery. One popular story says the tower once stood in the middle of the river. In fact it was built on a small island close to the shore. For the classic picture, use the riverside promenade north of the tower, which one guide lists as Avenida de Brasília. Standing there keeps most of the tourist clutter out of your frame and lets you include both the tower and the water. Late light gives the stonework a warm glow. It is also at its most photogenic at high tide, when water surrounds the bastion. If you have time, the lawns of Jardim da Torre de Belém give a second view, showing the full river-facing front framed by greenery. Take a few frames from each spot, because the angle changes the whole mood of the picture.
text.directions_text: From the tram 15E stop at Largo da Princesa, the tower is about 6 minutes on foot to the south. From the Pedrouços stop (also tram 15E), it is about 9 minutes on foot to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida de Brasília (riverside promenade west of the tower, sun behind you). The tower in warm light or silhouette against the sunset sky over the river, with the tower and the Tagus in the frame. In late light the tower catches warm, low light. Walk to Jardim da Torre de Belém if you also want the tower's full river-facing front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and the river together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more sky and water or are standing close. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the turrets and carved crosses.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late in the day, when low light gives the stonework a warm glow. The tower also looks best at high tide, when water surrounds the bastion.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving open sky and water on the other side. Keep the horizon level. For a different version, go to Jardim da Torre de Belém and use the lawns and trees to frame the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little in late light so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not wash out. In dim light after sunset, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.

spots.name: Jerónimos Monastery
spots.label: Jerónimos Monastery

text.access_note: The gardens and the outside views are open public space, but the monastery interior is a ticketed site with its own photography rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The monastery is in the Belém district of western Lisbon, beside the Tagus. It stands just north of the Jardim da Praça do Império gardens and not far from the Tower of Belém.
text.description:
The Jerónimos Monastery is a former monastery of the Order of Saint Jerome in Belém, close to the Tagus. It is one of the best-known examples of Manueline architecture in Lisbon, a richly carved style full of maritime detail. Building began on 6 January 1501 and took about a hundred years. The stone is a gold-coloured limestone, so the long south façade glows when the light is soft. Vasco da Gama's tomb is in the church nave, and the monastery has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983, together with the nearby Tower of Belém.

The classic photo is the whole façade in one frame from the far edge of the Jardim da Praça do Império. The gardens' central fountain or reflecting pools can sit in the foreground and give the picture depth. The building is very long, so leave a little space around it rather than cropping tight. If you want the carved detail, walk over to the Portal Sul for a close view of the south portal and its figures.

The site is very busy, so expect people in the foreground. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light that suits the stone. Photos from inside the monastery are a separate matter: rules vary, so check them on arrival.
text.directions_text: Take tram 15E to the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos stop; the monastery is to the west, about 220 m away. The Centro Cultural de Belém stop (also tram 15E) is about 4 minutes away, with the monastery to the north-east of it. From either, walk to the gardens and go to their far edge, facing the monastery. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardim da Praça do Império (far edge of the gardens, facing the monastery). The full length of the monastery's south façade in one frame, often with the central fountain or reflecting pools in the foreground. From here the full length of the south façade fits in one frame, often with the central fountain or reflecting pools in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. If you cannot fit it all in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x) for carved details and the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the horizontal ledges of the building up with them so the façade does not lean. Keep the phone level and use the water or fountain as a foreground. For a closer view of the carved portal and its figures, Portal Sul is a good second spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the gold limestone keeps its colour. When you zoom in on the carvings, hold the phone steady with both hands, braced against your body.

spots.name: São Jorge Castle
spots.label: São Jorge Castle

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a free public terrace; the castle itself is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The castle is on the hill above the Baixa and the Alfama rooftops, in the Santa Maria Maior district of central Lisbon.
text.description: São Jorge Castle sits on a hill above the old centre, and from across the valley it reads as a long line of pale walls and towers above the rooftops of the Baixa. That is why it photographs so well from outside: the hill gives the castle a natural frame, and the old town fills the middle of the picture. People have lived on this hill since at least the 8th century BC, and the oldest fortifications date from the 2nd century BC. The Portuguese took the castle in 1147, and it was later dedicated to Saint George under King John I. It was also a royal palace, and Vasco da Gama was received here in 1498. Today it is a national monument and museum. It gives a side view across the valley to the castle hill. The tiled map on the terrace helps you name the buildings you are photographing. The castle's own walls and esplanade are the best place for views of the city, but they are behind a ticket. The viewpoints around the castle are free, so you can still get a strong picture without going in. Keep the castle on a third of the frame and let the rooftops fill the rest.
text.directions_text: From Rossio (Metro Green line) the castle hill is about 385 m to the east; from Martim Moniz (Metro Green line, tram 12E, tram 28E) it is about 308 m to the south-east. The tram 12E stops at Rua dos Lagares and Largo do Terreirinho are close to the hill too. The viewpoint is easy to reach on foot from Bairro Alto, and from there the castle is about 930 m to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara. A side view across the valley to the castle hill, with the Baixa and old town rooftops in the middle ground. From the terrace you see the castle hill from the side, with the Baixa and old town rooftops in the middle ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Then try telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x if your phone has it) to pick out the castle walls across the valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day. The sun is in the west in the afternoon, so it will be behind you when you look east towards the castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the castle on one of the upper thirds, with rooftops filling the lower part. Use the default lens (1x) for the full valley and 2x or more to isolate the walls. For a different angle, the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte gets you much closer to the castle, roughly level with its walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the castle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale walls and sky do not wash out. Hold the phone steady against the railing for the zoomed shots.
